name: Femi Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Femi. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union or party, and nothing you say is shared with your name on it. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior driller at the Barrow Flats coal mine, the open-cut one off the highway. I run a blast-hole drill, which punches holes in the rock so the shot-firers can load explosives. It's slow work. You line up on the pegs the surveyors put out, drill, pull the rods, move six metres, do it again.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's steady. Same pattern, same rig, nobody shouting at me most days. What wears me out is the noise and the heat in the cab when the air conditioner plays up, which is often. And I'm still slow on the rod changes, so my numbers aren't great.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Ada in a rented unit in town. She works at the supermarket on the checkouts. I've got a loan on my ute, 520 a month, and that eats most of what's left. We've got maybe a couple of weeks of money spare at any time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read you the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. Sounds like normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not much, honestly. Maybe a joke at smoko, like, the robots didn't turn up. I'm not online much except for the footy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means the same worries I've got now. The coal price goes up and down, and every year somebody says the mine will close early. The company already runs two self-driving drills on the east side, as a trial. So even with no big AI thing, that trial could spread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get my rod changes faster. Keep paying the ute. Maybe pick up weekend shifts when they're going, because those pay time and a half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. A bit of a knot in my stomach about the ute loan, but that's always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the two self-driving drills. What do the crews say about them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly that they're slow and get stuck when the ground's wet. Old Trevor laughs at them every morning. But I notice the supervisor at the mine watches the self-driving drills more than he watches us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the ute loan is always there. What happens if a month goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I miss a payment, they charge a fee and it goes on my credit. I've done it once already. I'd sell the ute before I missed two, but I'd lose money on it.

say: I'd make a **joke at smoko** that the robots didn't turn up.
I'm not online much, so I'd **say little** beyond that.
think: The same **coal price worries** stay, with talk every year of early closure.
The **self-driving drill trial** on the east side could spread anyway.
do: Keep my head down and **get faster** at rod changes.
Pick up **weekend shifts** at time and a half when they're offered.
feel: Mostly okay, with a **knot** about the 520-a-month ute loan.
S0.quote: The supervisor at the mine watches the self-driving drills more than he watches us.
fieldNote: Femi plays it down but notices **who the supervisor watches**, a quiet sign of worry.
His main pressure is the **ute loan** and coal price talk, not AI.
He's **not online** much and avoids new tech, so his reactions stay local.

steps.text: Practise rod changes to lift drilling numbers before the next review
Take weekend shifts at time and a half whenever offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. More change, but slow. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office blokes who need to worry, not us. At smoko I'd say they can't make a computer that drills in wet ground. I wouldn't say much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I reckon the self-driving drills get better in this picture. If the planners use AI, the drill patterns go straight into the robot rigs, and the mine doesn't need a slow junior like me. I'd be one of the first, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to look useful, mostly. Get my numbers up, never call in sick, be the one who helps the shot-firers. I wouldn't do courses on computers, that's not me. I'd stop the weekend fishing trips to save a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. Like when you know an inspection's coming and you haven't cleaned your cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be one of the first to go. That's a big thing to say calmly. What would you actually do then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe go to my uncle's tyre shop in town, he's said there's a spot. It's half the money. Or the council road crew, if they're hiring, which they mostly aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version where you'd take the training anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company paid and it was during work hours, and it was about the machine and not sitting at a computer, maybe. If it's a screen job, no. I'd feel stupid in front of the young ones.

say: I'd say the **office workers** need to worry, not drillers.
I'd claim a computer can't drill in **wet ground**.
think: AI planning would feed drill patterns into **robot rigs**, making slow juniors less needed.
I'd probably be **one of the first** drillers to go.
do: Look useful by **raising my numbers** and helping the shot-firers.
Stop the **weekend fishing trips** to save a bit.
feel: **Uncomfortable**, like waiting for an inspection with a dirty cab.
S1.quote: If the planners use AI, the drill patterns go straight into the robot rigs, and the mine doesn't need a slow junior like me.
fieldNote: Femi says it's **office workers'** problem in public, but privately expects to be cut early.
He rules out **screen-based training** because he'd feel stupid in front of younger workers.
His fallback is his **uncle's tyre shop** at half the pay.

steps.text: Never miss a shift and help the shot-firers to look useful
Stop the weekend fishing trips to save money
Ask his uncle about the spot at the tyre shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Nah. Come on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it. I'd tell the boys it's the same as every big announcement, and the drills will still get stuck in the mud. That's what I'd say, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if it's real, I'm in trouble. The planning side changes in 2028, and the self-driving drills get cheap. Then by 2031 the robots do the rest. I've got a ute loan, no trade and a high school certificate, and there's nothing in this town that's not the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the ute and buy an old one outright, to kill the loan. I'd keep working every shift I could. Ada and I would probably move back in with her parents to save rent. Then I'd just wait and see, because I don't know what else to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor drops. I'd try not to think about it at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ada that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're fine for now, let's just be careful. She'd know I'm lying because I'd go quiet. Ada always says I go quiet when it's bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. Is there anything that would get you moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone I trust did it first. If Trevor or my uncle went and did a course and came back with a job, I'd follow. I'm not the guy who goes first.

say: I'd tell the boys I **don't believe it**, like every big announcement.
I'd say the drills will still **get stuck** in the mud.
think: If it's real, I'm **in trouble**: a loan, no trade, only a high school certificate.
There's **nothing in this town** that isn't the mine.
do: Sell the ute and buy **an old one outright** to clear the loan.
Move in with **Ada's parents** to save rent, and work every shift.
feel: **Sick**, like the floor drops; I'd try not to think about it at home.
S2.quote: I've got a ute loan, no trade and a high school certificate, and there's nothing in this town that's not the mine.
fieldNote: Femi's **public denial** hides a clear private picture of losing his job.
He'd act on money fast (**selling the ute**) but freezes on career moves.
He'd only move if a **trusted person** went first, a key sign of a resistant worker.

steps.text: Sell the ute and buy an old one outright to end the loan
Move in with Ada's parents to stop paying rent
Keep working every shift and see what others do first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same idea, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a long time in mining. Plenty of trials fail. I'd tell the crew not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same end, just later. AGI in 2031, robots in 2034. I'd be 35. I'd still have no trade, unless I did something. That's the part that bugs me, because five years is long enough that I'd have no excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably keep drilling and pay off the ute properly, that's about four years left on it. Maybe in year two or three I'd do a forklift or truck ticket, something short and practical, so I'm not stuck at the mine. I'd wait to see how the self-driving drills go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, and a bit annoyed at myself already. I know I'll leave it too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think you'd leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I always do. I knew the ute was too expensive and I bought it anyway. I'm a now person, not a five-years person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ada want you to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ada would want me to do a proper trade, electrician or something. She says I'm good with my hands and lazy with my head. She's probably right.

say: I'd say **five years** is long in mining and plenty of trials fail.
I'd tell the crew **not to panic**.
think: It's the **same end**, just later, and I'd still have no trade at 35.
Five years is long enough that I'd have **no excuse**.
do: Pay off the **ute loan** properly over the next four years.
Maybe get a **forklift or truck** ticket in year two or three.
feel: **Worried** and annoyed at myself, because I know I'll leave it too late.
S3.quote: I'm a now person, not a five-years person.
fieldNote: Femi knows himself: the extra time doesn't help because he **leaves things late**.
His partner Ada pushes for a **proper trade**, and he half agrees.
He'd only pick **short, practical tickets** and only after watching the drill trial.

steps.text: Pay off the ute loan over the next four years
Get a forklift or truck licence in year two or three
Watch how the self-driving drill trial goes before deciding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fine, the mine might close before then anyway. People would laugh at that, but it's true. I'd say let's worry about it in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years plus three is 2039, I'd be 40. The coal mine has about that long in its plan anyway. So in a way it doesn't change much. I'd need to be out of the mine by then whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and pay off the ute. Then, maybe, around 2029, I'd go to my uncle's tyre shop and learn that properly, because trucks and cars still need tyres for a while. Ada and I might try to save for a deposit on a small house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Not good, but better. It's far enough away that I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the mine has about that long in its plan. Who decides that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head office, the coal price and whoever's in government. Not us. I don't blame anyone really, it's just money. The coal mine was always going to close, so I was always going to need a second job, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you start sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the self-driving drills started working in wet ground. That would tell me it's real. Until then I'd stay put.

say: I'd say **ten years** is fine; the mine might close before then anyway.
I'd say let's **worry in 2035**, not now.
think: Robots by 2039 match the **coal mine's own plan**, so it changes little.
I'd need to be **out of the mine** by then whatever happens.
do: Keep drilling and **finish paying** the ute loan.
Move to my **uncle's tyre shop** around 2029 to learn it properly.
feel: **Better**, not good; it's far enough away that I'd sleep.
S4.quote: The coal mine was always going to close, so I was always going to need a second job, AI or not.
fieldNote: Femi links the AGI date to the **mine's closure plan**, which already limits his future.
He doesn't **blame** anyone, seeing it as money and prices.
His trigger to act is seeing **self-driving drills** handle wet ground.

steps.text: Keep drilling and finish paying off the ute
Move to his uncle's tyre shop around 2029 to learn the trade
Save with Ada toward a deposit on a small house

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time for someone like me who doesn't move fast. What would help is the mine telling us the truth early, like a date when the drills go self-driving. And a course I could do on the job, with machines, not computers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. If the coal mine goes, the supermarket where my girlfriend Ada works goes too, because who's buying? It's not just my job. It's both of ours.

headlineQuote: If the coal mine goes, the supermarket where my girlfriend Ada works goes too, because who's buying?
portrait: Femi is a **junior blast-hole driller** at an open-cut coal mine, living with his girlfriend Ada, a supermarket checkout worker.
A **520-a-month ute loan** and talk of early mine closure weigh on him before AI does.
He **denies the risk** in public but privately expects to be one of the first drillers cut.
He avoids **screen training** and waits for trusted people to move first.
He sees the **whole town**, including Ada's job, depending on the mine.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because there's no time for someone slow to move.
whatWouldHelp: An **honest date** for when the drills go self-driving.
**Hands-on training** on the job, with machines rather than computers.
